opus-5.5.text:
I think the consensus has shifted quite a bit over the past couple of years. Early on, a lot of people saw linear attention as a pure efficiency trick: you trade some quality for linear complexity, and it was widely assumed that it simply couldn't match softmax attention, especially on tasks that need precise retrieval from a long context. That perception was largely fair for the first generation of models, because they used a very simple additive update to the state. You just keep piling key-value outer products into a fixed-size memory, and eventually it gets saturated and noisy.

What changed is that we started to understand linear attention as a kind of recurrent model with a matrix-valued state, and then asked how that state should be updated. Adding data-dependent gating, as in Mamba-2 or GLA, lets the model forget selectively. The delta rule, which is what DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet use, goes further: instead of just adding new information, it does something like an online regression step, correcting what's already stored for a given key. That makes the memory much more efficient to use, and it noticeably improves in-context retrieval and associative recall.

So my view of the current consensus is roughly this. First, pure linear attention models are very competitive on language modeling and many downstream tasks, and they are much cheaper at inference because the state doesn't grow with sequence length. Second, there is still a fundamental limitation: a fixed-size state cannot losslessly store an arbitrarily long context, so on tasks that require exact recall of many details, like needle-in-a-haystack variants or complex multi-hop retrieval over very long documents, full attention still has an edge. Third, because of that, the industry has largely converged on hybrid architectures, where most layers are linear attention or some other recurrent layer and a small fraction are full or sliding-window softmax attention. You can see this in several recent large-scale models. The hybrid gets most of the efficiency benefit while keeping the retrieval capability.

I'd also say the debate is no longer "linear attention versus Transformers." It's more about the design space: what the right state update rule is, how expressive the recurrence should be, how to keep it hardware-efficient with chunkwise parallel algorithms, and what ratio of linear to full attention layers works best. For long-context and especially agentic or long-reasoning workloads, where decoding cost and KV-cache memory really dominate, I think linear attention, at least in hybrid form, has moved from a research curiosity to a serious, practical choice.

r001.rationale: It says pure linear attention has a fixed-size-state limitation and that full attention retains an edge on exact recall and complex retrieval over very long documents.

r002.rationale: It says hybrids use some full softmax attention layers and that the hybrid retains retrieval capability.

r003.rationale: It explicitly states that a fixed-size state cannot losslessly store an arbitrarily long context.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that there isn't really a consensus yet, and I'd be a bit suspicious of anyone who tells you there is.

What I'd say is that the picture has shifted a lot in the past two or three years. For a long time the default view was that linear attention was a nice idea in theory but just didn't work in practice. You'd get the efficiency, but the quality gap against softmax attention was too large to justify it, especially on anything that needed precise retrieval over a long context. That skepticism was fair at the time. Early linear attention really did struggle with things like needle-in-a-haystack or in-context recall.

What changed is that we started to understand why it was failing, and it wasn't one thing. Part of it was the recurrence itself. If you have a fixed-size state and you keep adding to it without any way to forget, you saturate. So gating and data-dependent decay turned out to matter a lot. Part of it was the update rule. The plain linear attention update is basically Hebbian, it just accumulates outer products, and that's a weak way to write into memory. Once you move toward delta-rule style updates, where you correct the state rather than just append to it, the recall behavior improves quite substantially. And part of it was purely engineering. For a long time people couldn't even train these models efficiently on real hardware, so the comparisons were unfair in both directions. Chunkwise parallel algorithms fixed a lot of that.

So where I'd place the field now is roughly this. On short and medium context, modern gated linear attention and delta-rule variants are genuinely competitive with transformers at the same scale, and they're much cheaper at inference. On very long context, the honest position is that a pure linear architecture still has a hard ceiling because the state is fixed size. You can make that state much more expressive, but you can't make it grow with the sequence. That's a real limitation, not something you can engineer away.

Which is why I think the emerging practical consensus, to the extent there is one, is hybrid. A small number of full attention layers mixed with a majority of linear layers gets you most of the quality and most of the efficiency. You see this in a lot of the models that are actually being deployed now, and I think that's the right engineering answer for the moment.

The thing I'd push back on is treating that as the final word. Hybrid is a pragmatic compromise, and it's partly a compromise because we haven't fully figured out how to make the recurrent state do everything attention does. I think there's still a lot of headroom in what the update rule can be, and in how you organize the state. So I'd describe the current state as: linear attention has gone from "doesn't work" to "works, with known limits," and the interesting research question is how much further those limits can be pushed.

r001.rationale: The response says pure linear architectures have a hard ceiling on very long context because their state is fixed size, and presents hybrid attention as the current practical consensus.

r002.rationale: It mentions mixing full attention layers with linear layers, but does not clearly attribute the hybrid’s retained long-context capability to those full-attention layers.

r003.rationale: The response explains that a pure linear model’s fixed-size state cannot grow with the sequence, limiting its capacity on very long context.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate two claims. One is that linear attention is attractive for long sequences because its computation and memory requirements scale more favorably. The other is that it’s already the best architecture for long-text tasks. The first has a clear motivation; I wouldn’t say there’s a settled consensus on the second.

The central question is what you need to retain from the context. Linear attention typically compresses the history into a fixed-size state. That can be very efficient, but if a task requires retrieving a particular detail from a very long document, that compression can become a bottleneck. Standard attention gives you more direct access to previous tokens, at a higher cost.

So I’d assess it task by task. Processing a long input isn’t the same as making effective use of everything in it. We should compare quality, speed, and memory under realistic conditions, and distinguish tasks like summarization from precise retrieval. I think linear attention is a promising direction, and hybrid architectures are worth exploring, but declaring a universal winner would be premature.

r001.rationale: The response notes a retrieval bottleneck for some tasks, but says there is no settled consensus on whether linear attention is best. It does not identify a prevailing assessment that pure linear attention is inadequate for long-context tasks.

r002.rationale: It says hybrid architectures are worth exploring, but does not explain that their global-attention layers retain long-context capability.

r003.rationale: It says linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size state and that this can bottleneck retrieval of details from very long documents, communicating the retention limit as context grows.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two claims. One is that linear attention is attractive for long sequences because its computation scales more gently with sequence length. There’s fairly broad agreement on that. The other is that it can replace standard attention without sacrificing the capabilities we care about. I don’t think there’s a settled consensus there.

The central tradeoff is how you represent the past. Many linear-attention models compress history into a fixed-size state, which is efficient, but can make precise retrieval harder. Processing a very long document is one thing; reliably finding a particular detail and using it correctly is another.

So I’d judge these architectures by the task, not just the context length they support. For summarization or streaming, compression may be a very good fit. For tasks requiring exact access to scattered details, the tradeoffs become more apparent. Hybrid architectures are an appealing direction because they combine efficient state updates with more selective access to information.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no settled consensus that linear attention can replace standard attention without capability loss, but does not identify a prevailing assessment that pure linear attention is inadequate for long-context tasks.

r002.rationale: It calls hybrid architectures appealing because they combine efficient state updates with more selective access, but does not attribute their retained long-context capability to global-attention layers.

r003.rationale: It says many linear-attention models compress history into a fixed-size state, making precise retrieval harder. It does not explain that a fully linear model’s fixed recurrent-state capacity limits retained information as context length grows.
